case_study_insert.main_stem: Orchardale Beverages (OAB) is a public limited company in the soft drinks and fruit juice manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 72. Founded in 1998 by Marcus Orchardale, it supplies cold-pressed juice to national retailers and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. OAB plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new cold-pressed juice bottling line, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.00 a unit and a selling price of $10.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. OAB faces two problems: packaging waste has reached 3.4% and customer quality complaints are rising across the bottling floor.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q4 2025: The cold-pressed line filled 28,000 bottles last quarter with a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 3.8% a year ago. Customer quality complaints fell from 51 to 33 per month. Average delivery time to retailers is 3.4 days. Packaging waste measured 3.4% of output. A pilot team working scheme cut line stoppages by 18%. A survey of 800 shoppers found 66% would pay up to $0.60 more for cold-pressed juice and 58% choose drinks by brand reputation. Training records show 24 of 72 staff still need on-the-job training on the new filler; off-the-job training at the local institute costs $1,000 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Orchardale Beverages as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $13.40 to $14.22 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Fruit and packaging input costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is 6.9%, while consumer spending on cold-pressed juice grew 5.3% in the same period.

questions.question_text: OAB plans to fund part of its bottling expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for OAB of using a share issue instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $500,000 share issue raises permanent capital that carries no interest payments or capital repayments, unlike the $700,000 bank loan, so OAB's cash flow is protected while it already meets fixed costs of $360,000 a year. The new equity can fund the $1,200,000 bottling line directly and help absorb the 10.2% rise in fruit and packaging costs without pushing the $10.00 selling price above what national retailers will accept.

Point 2: Share issue finance does not require collateral, so OAB's other assets are not at risk of repossession if sales of cold-pressed juice disappoint. It also spreads ownership among new shareholders rather than leaving Marcus Orchardale dependent on a lender that could impose conditions on how the business is run. As a public limited company, OAB can access a wide pool of investors, making a share issue a practical way to raise the $500,000 needed. Overall, equity is cheaper in cash-flow terms and less risky than adding to the company's bank debt.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to OAB and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: OAB is launching its new cold-pressed juice range. Consider a television advertising campaign, sponsorship of a sports event, or social media influencer marketing. Which should OAB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television advertising campaign: Television would give the cold-pressed juice range mass reach very quickly across national retailers. However, production and airtime costs are high for a 72-employee firm already funding a $1,200,000 bottling line with a $700,000 loan, and a broad audience includes many people who do not buy cold-pressed juice, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Sponsorship of a sports event: Sponsorship can build strong brand reputation and healthy associations that match the 58% of surveyed shoppers who choose drinks by brand reputation. It is costlier than influencer work and harder to measure, and a single event gives a short burst of exposure rather than the sustained education a new cold-pressed product needs.

Social media influencer marketing: Health and food influencers can demonstrate cold-pressed juice to a targeted audience at a low cost per reached shopper, and can speak directly to the 66% of 800 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.60 more for the product. Results take time to compound and depend on influencer credibility, but the message supports the premium positioning.

Recommendation: OAB should choose social media influencer marketing as the lead channel, with a small sports sponsorship later. Influencers reach the exact health-conscious segment identified in the research, cost far less than television, and can justify the $0.60 premium nationally. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a firm servicing a $700,000 loan, and sponsorship is rejected as expensive, short-lived and less measurable than influencer activity for a new juice launch.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of OAB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of OAB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: OAB's packaging waste has reached 3.4% and quality complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for OAB of using team working to improve performance on the bottling line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets the 72 employees share ideas about reducing the 3.4% packaging waste, since the operators who run the filler know where bottles and labels are damaged. The pilot team working scheme already cut line stoppages by 18%, showing that joint problem-solving can raise efficiency and protect the $6.00 contribution per unit under a laissez-faire structure.

Point 2: Working in teams spreads skill and covers for absence, so output of 120,000 units is less disrupted when a worker is off, and shared responsibility improves quality control, helping to reverse rising customer complaints and the 2.6% defect rate. Higher involvement also raises motivation and can reduce the need for the $1,000 per employee off-the-job training, because experienced team members coach newer staff on the job.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to OAB's waste, quality and output.

questions.question_text: OAB must upskill 24 filling-line staff to operate the new bottling machinery. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local institute. Which should OAB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training 24 staff on OAB's own filler is directly relevant to the company's exact machine settings and quality standards, costs nothing in external fees, and keeps those workers productive while they learn, protecting output toward 120,000 units and the aim of cutting the 2.6% defect rate. The drawback is that trainers are themselves production staff whose output suffers, and bad habits can be passed on, which matters while quality complaints are rising.

Off-the-job training: The local institute course at $1,000 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate for all 24 staff, costing $24,000 in total — small beside the $1,200,000 investment. It removes 24 workers from the line, cutting short-term capacity and risking more packaging waste, and the generic content may not match OAB's exact filler, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: OAB should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, adding short institute modules later for senior operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing capacity while waste is at 3.4% and complaints are rising; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing $24,000 and 24 staff from a new line would jeopardise supply to national retailers, and OAB can add certification once the bottling line is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to OAB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of OAB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of OAB with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how OAB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($10.00 − $4.00) = $360,000 ÷ $6.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $10.00 − $4.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways OAB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. OAB's managers can compare the 60,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 120,000 units to confirm the bottling line is profitable, giving a margin of safety of 60,000 units, which supports running the new $1,200,000 line at capacity.
2. Contribution per unit of $6.00 lets OAB model the $0.60 premium for cold-pressed juice: if won, contribution rises toward $6.60, showing how much extra volume is needed to cover $360,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $360,000 and contribution of $6.00 lets managers set the sales volume needed to service the $700,000 bank loan and check the line can afford repayments before committing more equity.
4. Managers can use unit cost ($360,000 ÷ 120,000 units + $4.00 = $7.00 a unit) to benchmark each quarter, isolate the 3.4% packaging waste, and judge whether to renegotiate the $4.00 variable cost given 10.2% fruit and packaging inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 120,000-unit output; the $0.60 premium against $360,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $700,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $7.00 to tackle 3.4% packaging waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate OAB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has OAB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.52 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.08 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $180,000 inventories + $140,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $380,000; 2025 current assets = $160,000 + $170,000 + $100,000 = $430,000. Liquidity cover for 2024 = $380,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.52, and for 2025 = $430,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.72. Excluding stock, 2024 = ($380,000 − $180,000) ÷ $250,000 = $200,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.80, and 2025 = ($430,000 − $160,000) ÷ $250,000 = $270,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.08.

Evaluation: OAB's short-term liquidity has strengthened. The first ratio rose from 1.52 to 1.72 as current assets grew from $380,000 to $430,000 while current liabilities stayed at $250,000, so the firm covers its short-term debts more comfortably. The second ratio, which strips out inventories, improved from 0.80 to 1.08, so OAB is less dependent on selling juice stock to meet obligations — useful while it services a $700,000 bank loan and builds a $1,200,000 bottling line. However, trade receivables rose from $140,000 to $170,000, tying up cash; if national retailers pay late the position could weaken, and the fall in inventories to $160,000 should be watched to avoid stockouts.

Conclusion: OAB's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures moved favourably (1.52 to 1.72 and 0.80 to 1.08), and the improvement does not rely on stock. The residual risk is higher receivables, so OAB should tighten credit control with retailers while proceeding with the bottling investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether OAB's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for OAB of positioning its new range as cold-pressed juice.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Cold-pressed juice matches the preferences of the 66% of 800 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.60 more, letting OAB charge a premium that protects the $6.00 contribution per unit even as fruit and packaging costs rise 10.2%. It also supports the 58% who choose drinks by brand reputation, helping win and keep listings with national retailers for the $1,200,000 bottling line.

Disadvantage: Cold-pressed juice typically has a shorter shelf life and higher production cost than standard juice, which could keep the $4.00 variable cost per unit high and worsen the 3.4% packaging waste if more bottles are returned. Any quality slip would deepen the customer complaints already rising on the bottling line, and the premium depends on shoppers accepting the higher price.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to OAB's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in input costs will affect OAB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If OAB's $700,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75 percentage points × $700,000 = $5,250 a year (0.0075 × $700,000). That is modest against $360,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may also make consumers cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing, but OAB can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $14.22 an hour): OAB employs a workforce of 72 in bottling and packing, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay figures are given, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented; the honest test is productivity: 120,000 units ÷ 72 staff = 1,666.67 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $6.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (10.2% fruit and packaging): OAB's $4.00 variable cost per unit contains fruit and packaging, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.2% that adds about 10.2% × $4.00 = $0.41 per unit, and at 120,000 units that is roughly $49,000 a year. Even a smaller rise erodes contribution, but the $0.60 premium and retailer price talks can recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 10.2% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 120,000 bottles and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $1,200,000 line, and unlike the loan it cannot be neutralised by fixing a rate. The wage rise is real but manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only about $5,250, so both are smaller.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to OAB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on OAB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of OAB with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
